Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Specify the epidemiology of distal humerus fractures and the anatomy of the distal humerus.
Perform an appropriate workup of patients with a distal humerus fracture.
Identify the fracture patterns and classification systems for distal humerus factures.
Understand the nonsurgical and surgical management of distal humerus fractures.
Understand the surgical approaches and indications for an olecranon osteotomy.
Understand the principles of surgical fixation of distal humerus fractures and the
complications associated with surgical management.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Epidemiology
Intercondylar fractures are the most common distal humerus fracture pattern.

Fractures of the capitellum constitute approximately 1% of all elbow injuries.
Fractures of a single condyle account for 5% of all distal humerus fractures, with lateral
condyle fractures being more common than medial condyle fractures.

Epidemiology
Distal humerus fractures account for 2% of all fractures in adults, with an incidence of 43
cases per 100,000 persons per year.1 These fractures range from simple, extra-articular
fractures to isolated coronal shear fractures of the articular surface or complex intra-
articular fractures with metaphyseal or articular comminution. Distal humerus fractures
have a bimodal distribution with respect to age and sex, with peak occurrence in males
aged 12 to 19 years and females aged 80 years or older.2,3
Fractures of the capitellum are uncommon and account for approximately 6% of
fractures involving the distal humerus and approximately 1% of all elbow fractures.4
Coronal shear fractures of capitellum often occur during a fall onto an outstretched arm,
resulting in direct axial compression of the capitellum by the radial head or spontaneous
reduction of a posterolateral dislocation. Therefore, concomitant injuries to the lateral
collateral ligament or radial head may be present in as many as 57% of patients with a
capitellar fracture.5
Anatomy and Biomechanics
(Figure 1) and (Figure 2); Resources 1 and 2)
The articular surface of the distal humerus is in 6° of valgus, 5° of external rotation, and 30° of
flexion relative to the long axis of the humerus.
The ulnar nerve lies posterior to the medial epicondyle within the cubital tunnel.
The distal humerus has an extraosseous and intraosseous blood supply that may be
compromised with extensive subperiosteal elevation or disrupted from the injury.

Anatomy and Biomechanics

The elbow is a constrained, hinged joint consisting of the articulation between the distal
humerus, ulna, and radius. The distal humerus is composed of the medial and lateral
columns, the epicondyles, and the articular surface (trochlea and capitellum). Proximal
to the trochlea are the olecranon and coronoid fossae, which consist primarily of thin,
cortical bone and are often comminuted in patients with a distal humerus fracture. The
ulna rotates around the axis of the trochlea and is positioned in relative valgus and
external rotation. The capitellum articulates with the proximal radius and is involved
with forearm rotation. The ulnar nerve resides in the cubital tunnel and exits the elbow
through the flexor carpi ulnaris. The blood supply to the distal humerus consists of
extraosseous and intraosseous vessels that form three vascular arcades: medial, lateral,
and posterior.6, 7 The medial arcade is formed by the superior ulnar collateral artery,
inferior ulnar collateral artery, and posterior ulnar recurrent artery and supplies the
medial epicondyle, medial aspect of the trochlea, and posteromedial aspect of the
olecranon. The blood supply to the lateral epicondyle, capitellum, and lateral trochlea
comes from the lateral arcade, which arises from the radial recurrent, radial collateral,
and interosseus recurrent arteries. These arteries, which penetrate the distal humerus
posterior and superior to the capitellum, may be injured with excessive subperiosteal
dissection and contribute the risk of nonunion and osteonecrosis.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Distal humerus fractures may result from high- or low-energy mechanisms of injury, especially
in patients with osteoporotic bone.
The fracture pattern may be influenced by the amount of elbow flexion at the time of injury.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Distal humerus fractures in younger patients often result from high-energy mechanisms
of injury, such as motor vehicle accidents, falls from height, gunshot wounds, or sports-
related injuries. Geriatric distal humerus fractures result from low-energy mechanisms
of injury, such as a fall from standing height. Transcolumnar fractures result from an
axial load directed through the forearm with the elbow flexed 90°. A similar elbow
position and direct impact on the olecranon may result in an olecranon fracture with or
without a distal humerus fracture. An intercondylar fracture may occur with the elbow in
more than 90° of flexion.
Associated Injuries
Ipsilateral forearm or proximal humerus fractures may occur at the time of injury.
Signs and symptoms of ulnar neuropathy, such as numbness, weakness, or pain, may be
present preoperatively.

Associated Injuries
Although rare, ipsilateral forearm fractures, such as Monteggia injuries, olecranon
fractures, coronoid fractures, radial head fractures, and ipsilateral proximal humerus
fractures, may occur in combination with distal humerus fractures. A complete series of

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004099
6/37

radiographs of the forearm and humerus in addition to radiographs of the elbow are
crucial during the initial evaluation. Ulnar nerve injury also may be present at the time of
injury; however, the true incidence of ulnar nerve injury is poorly documented.8 In a
study of 117 patients with a complete articular distal humerus fracture, Ruan et al9
reported that 29 patients (24.8%) had symptoms of preoperative ulnar neuropathy.
Patients must be carefully evaluated preoperatively for any signs or symptoms of ulnar
neuropathy because the presence of numbness, pain, or weakness may influence
management of the ulnar nerve.
Injury Classification
Classifications of fractures of the distal humerus traditionally were descriptive and based on
the number of columns involved and the location of the fracture (Table 1).
The AO Foundation/Orthopaedic Trauma Association classification system divides distal
humerus fractures into type A (extra-articular), type B (partial articular), and type C (complete
articular) fractures (Figure 3; Resource 3).
Isolated lateral condyle fractures are characterized according to the Milch classification, which
describes the stability of the fracture pattern (Figure 4).
Several classification schemes describe articular shear fractures of the capitellum and/or
trochlea; however, none have been reported to reliably indicate management or predict
outcome (Figures 5 and 6; Resource 4).


Injury Classification
Distal humerus fractures as described by the AO Foundation/Orthopaedic Trauma
Association classification are denoted by the number 13 (1: humerus, 3: distal end
segment). The letter following the number indicates the type of fracture: extra-articular
(type A), partial articular (type B), or complete articular (type C). Each category is then
subclassified based on the fracture pattern and degree and location of fracture
comminution. The AO Foundation/Orthopaedic Trauma Association classification is
associated with substantial stand-alone agreement for interobserver reliability for
fracture type (A, B, and C) but is less reliable for subtype.
The Milch classification system describes lateral condyle fractures and determines
fracture stability based on injury pattern. In type I fractures, the lateral wall of the
trochlea is attached to the main portion of the humerus. Type I fractures are stable
compared with type II fractures, in which the lateral wall of the trochlea is attached to
the displaced fragment.
Several classification systems have been used to describe articular shear fractures.4,5,10
Bryan and Morrey4 originally described three types of capitellar fractures, and McKee et
al10 later added a fourth type to describe injuries that extend into the trochlea.
Type I (Hahn-Steinthal fragment): These fractures involve a large osseous component
of the capitellum that may involve the trochlea.
Type II (Kocher-Lorenz fragment): These fractures are separations of articular cartilage
with minimal attached subchondral bone.
Type III (Broberg-Morrey variant): These are severely comminuted, multifragmentary
fractures.
Type IV: These fractures extend medially into the trochlea.
Dubberley et al5 proposed a different classification scheme that describes three types of
articular fractures, which were then characterized by the absence (subtype A) or
presence (subtype B) of posterior condylar comminution. The authors state that their

classification scheme provides some guidance for surgical management in addition to

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
The initial evaluation of distal humerus fractures begins with a thorough patient history and
physical examination.
A careful neurovascular examination must be performed to assess for preoperative nerve or
vascular injury.
Inspect the elbow, especially posteriorly, for open wounds or continuous venous oozing that
may suggest an open fracture.

Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients typically present with elbow pain, swelling, and deformity. Crepitus or gross
instability with attempted elbow range of motion (ROM) often is observed. A careful
neurovascular examination should be performed because all neurovascular structures
to the forearm and hand cross the area of injury, and sharp bone fragments can cause
damage, especially to the radial nerve, ulnar nerve, and brachial artery. Fracture blisters
or excessive swelling and pain may indicate an evolving compartment syndrome.
Imaging Studies
Complete radiographic series of the elbow, humerus, and forearm is necessary to properly
assess the degree of injury (Figure 7).
Traction radiographs and CT scans may aid in preoperative planning.

Imaging Studies
AP and lateral radiographs of the humerus and elbow are required. If concomitant elbow
injuries are present, then forearm and wrist radiographs may be necessary. A double-arc
sign, created by the capitellum and lateral trochlear ridge, is pathognomonic for a
coronal shear fracture of the distal humerus10-12 (Figure 8). After splint immobilization,
CT scans of the elbow may be extremely helpful in preoperative planning, especially in
patients with fractures that involve the articular surface and if three-dimensional

of articular injury and the need for olecranon osteotomy.

fracture. A, Preoperative lateral radiograph demonstrates the double-arc sign. AP (B) and

Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Trauma, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 275-293.)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management of distal humerus fractures is considered in low-demand patients
who have medical comorbidities that outweigh the advantages of surgical treatment (Video 1).

Video 1
King GJW: Nonsurgical treatment of distal humerus fractures in the older aged patient, from
Jupiter JB, mod: Contemporary issues with the management of distal humerus fractures in the
older aged patient. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.

Indications
Nonsurgical treatment of patients with distal humerus fractures is reserved for those
with clinical comorbidities that outweigh the advantages of a surgical procedure.
Nonsurgical treatment also is considered in patients who have limited use of the arm
because of an underlying neurologic condition and patients with a nondisplaced
fracture. Rates of nonunion with nonsurgical management range from 0% to 17% in the
literature.2,13
Contraindications
High-functioning patients or those with displaced fractures of the medial and lateral columns
Open fractures or associated neurovascular injuries

Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management of nondisplaced distal humerus fractures requires close monitoring
via weekly radiographs to assess for interval displacement.
Nonsurgical treatment of patients with a displaced distal humerus fracture includes cast/splint
immobilization with the elbow in 90° of flexion for 2 weeks, followed by early gentle ROM.

Techniques/Procedures
Nondisplaced fractures, especially low transcondylar fractures, should be closely
monitored because they are prone to rotational and sagittal plane deformity.14 Close
follow-up for the first few weeks via radiographs must be done to assess for interval
fracture displacement. In patients with a supracondylar humerus fracture, condylar shaft
angle loss of as much as 20° may be acceptable. Patients with an epicondylar fracture
that is nondisplaced who have a stable elbow joint during ROM also may be treated
nonsurgically. Gentle passive elbow motion may be initiated to prevent stiffness after a
period of immobilization or if radiographs demonstrate signs of healing. For patients
with an intercondylar fracture who are medically unfit, the nonsurgical bag-of-bones
treatment method may be used. This involves approximately 2 weeks of immobilization
with the elbow in 90° of flexion, followed by gentle ROM to ultimately achieve a
minimally painful, functional pseudarthrosis.
Outcomes
Nonsurgical management of distal humerus fractures may lead to good results in the
appropriate patient population with an appropriate fracture pattern.
Rates of nonunion after nonsurgical management range from zero to 17%.
In low-demand patients with clinical comorbidities, nonsurgical treatment may result in a
painless functional elbow.13,15,16
Surgical Management
Indications

9/3/26, 3:59 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004099
17/37

Surgical treatment is indicated for most patients with a displaced distal humerus fracture and
patients with an open fracture or neurovascular injury.
Contraindications
Closed fractures in low-demand patients who are medically frail and have comorbidities that
outweigh the advantages of surgical fixation
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Careful review of the injury radiographs, traction radiographs, and preoperative CT scans is
critical in determining the best surgical approach, reduction sequence, and fixation strategies.
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction may enhance knowledge of all the fracture fragments
and improve preoperative planning.
Patient Positioning
Patient positioning is dependent on the surgical approach.
The posterior approach to the distal humerus may be performed with the patient in the lateral
decubitus, prone, or supine position.
The lateral approach to the distal humerus for the management of articular shear fractures is
performed with the patient in the supine position.

Patient Positioning
Patients may be placed in the lateral decubitus, prone, or supine position for a posterior
approach to the distal humerus. For the lateral decubitus position, the patient is placed
on a radiolucent table and positioned laterally. An axillary roll may be used to avoid
pressure on the down arm and the brachial plexus. Prior to preparation of the arm, AP
and lateral C-arm images should be obtained to ensure appropriate images can be
obtained intraoperatively. The posterior approach to the distal humerus also may be
performed with the patient in the supine position. Patients are placed supine on a
regular surgical table, and the arm is draped over a sterile, padded Mayo stand. This
positioning avoids the risk of compressive nerve injuries resulting from lateral decubitus
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:59 PM
AAOS | Distal Humerus Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004099
18/37

positioning; however, it requires another assistant to help stabilize the arm
intraoperatively. C-arm imaging also may be easier to perform with the patient in the
supine position.
An isolated lateral approach to the elbow typically is used in patients placed in the
supine position, using a radiolucent hand table extension.
The use of a tourniquet during surgery depends on surgeon preference.
Surgical Approaches (Video 2)
All extra-articular and intra-articular distal humerus fractures are managed via a posterior
approach.
Management of the triceps depends on the fracture pattern and the amount of exposure
necessary to reduce the fracture and apply fixation.
An olecranon osteotomy may be required for adequate exposure and access to the articular
fragments.
Capitellar fractures may be managed via a Kocher or Kaplan approach.

Surgical Approaches
Extra-articular and partial articular fractures typically are approached via a posterior
triceps-splitting or paratricipital (triceps-sparing) approach. For a triceps-splitting
approach, a posterior incision is made and carried deep to the triceps, which is
subsequently split between the long and lateral heads and distally at its ulnar insertion.
Most surgeons will end the distal extent of the split at the tip of the olecranon; however,
the exposure can be continued distally to elevate the triceps off the ulna and repaired as
necessary (Video 3).
Video 3
McKee MD: Triceps-splitting approach for distal humeral fractures, from Kandemir U,
mod: Distal humerus fractures: Surgical techniques. Presented at the Annual Meeting of
the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.
The paratricipital approach involves mobilization of the triceps off the posterior humerus
from the medial and lateral aspects of the intermuscular septum, avoiding violation of
the extensor mechanism. Improved visualization of the articular surface may be

achieved by releasing the posterior bundle of the medial collateral ligament. The ulnar
nerve (medially) and the radial nerve (laterally and proximally) are identified and
protected. Dissection of the ulnar nerve may be continued distally to the first motor
branch of the flexor carpi ulnaris. Care should be taken to avoid devascularization of the
ulnar nerve during mobilization. The radial nerve can be located by retracting the triceps
medially to expose the lower lateral brachial cutaneous nerve that branches off the
radial nerve and then traced proximally to identify the radial nerve proper (Video 4).

For an isolated lateral column or capitellar fracture, a lateral (Kocher or Kaplan)
approach may be considered (Video 5).

Complex articular injury may require direct visualization through an olecranon
osteotomy, which provides the best overall view of the trochlea and capitellum (Video 6).
The ulnar nerve should be found and freed before performing an olecranon osteotomy.
A chevron-style osteotomy pointing distally is made at the level of the bare area of the
olecranon, approximately 2.5 to 3 cm from the tip of the olecranon. Fixation can be
placed before performing the olecranon osteotomy to facilitate fixation during
osteotomy repair. The osteotomy is begun with the use of an oscillating saw and
completed with the use of an osteotome to avoid injury to the adjacent cartilage surface
and thermal necrosis of the subchondral bone. The apex of the chevron should point
distally to ensure a larger proximal fragment. After the osteotomy is complete, the
extensor mechanism can be reflected proximally to allow for visualization of the entire
distal humerus.

Osteotomy repair can be performed with the use of Kirschner wires and a tension band;
a long, large-fragment intramedullary screw with a washer; or a plate and screws. In a
recent study comparing tension band and plate fixation for olecranon osteotomy repair,
no difference was found in overall elbow arc motion, time to union, Mayo Elbow
Performance Index score, or postoperative complications.17 Patients who underwent
tension band fixation had less of an extension deficit at final follow-up compared with
those who underwent plate fixation (10° versus 17°; P = 0.001). An olecranon osteotomy
should be avoided in older patients in whom conversion to total elbow arthroplasty (TEA)
may be required.
Surgical Techniques
The goal of surgery is to obtain anatomic reduction of the articular surface and restore length,
alignment, and rotation of the distal humerus.
Stable fixation of distal humerus fractures must be achieved to allow for safe, early range of
elbow motion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:59 PM
AAOS | Distal Humerus Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004099
23/37

For complete articular (AO Foundation/Orthopaedic Trauma Association type13C) fractures,
reduction sequence strategies include transforming a type C fracture to a type A or type B
fracture and then reducing the remaining fragment to the intact humeral shaft. Open
reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of intercondylar distal humerus fractures typically is
performed via bicolumnar fixation with the use of plates on the medial and lateral columns
(Video 7).
Although parallel locked plating is biomechanically stronger than orthogonal (90-90) plating,
both constructs can provide adequate stability, and no difference exists between the clinical
outcomes of the two plating methods.
TEA should be considered for comminuted intra-articular distal humerus fractures in patients
older than 65 years, particularly if they have low functional demands, medical comorbidities,
or poor bone quality.
Type I capitellar fractures can be fixed with the use of countersunk or headless compression
screws placed in an anterior-to-posterior or posterior-to-anterior fashion.

Surgical Techniques
The primary goals of surgical management are to achieve anatomic reduction of the
articular fragments; restore the length, rotation, and alignment of the distal humerus;
and achieve stable fixation to allow for early motion of the elbow. O’Driscoll18 describes
two principles to achieve stable fixation: fixation in the distal fragment must be
maximized, and all fixation in distal fragments should contribute to the stability of the
shaft and distal fragments.
The sequence of fracture reduction requires reassembly of articular fragments and
reconnection to the humeral shaft without compromising the required shape, width, and
depth of the articulating surfaces. Reduction of the articular segments may be achieved
with the use of pointed reduction clamps. Small-diameter Kirschner wires also may be
placed into fragments to allow for joystick manipulation of the fragments. Provisional
fixation of the articular segments can be achieved with the use of independent 2.4-mm
or 2.7-mm screws. Reduction of the articular block or condylar fragment can be achieved
with the use of reduction clamps, and provisional fixation is achieved with the use of
Kirschner wires placed up along the column or mini-fragment plates and screws placed
on the dorsal surface of the medial/lateral columns.
Locked plating is preferred in patients with poor bone quality and fracture comminution,
and plates may be placed parallel or orthogonal (90-90) to one another.19 Parallel plating
allows for distal screw interdigitation and anchors both columns to the humeral shaft,
forming the arch keystone; however, it may cause skin irritation because of the lateral
plate and extensive soft-tissue dissection laterally and medially. Orthogonal plating
provides resistance to force during elbow flexion, and placement of a posterolateral
plate is easier than placement of a lateral plate because less muscle and ligament
attachment is present on the posterior surface of the humerus. Disadvantages of
orthogonal plating include less resistance of varus loading and less compression
generated between the metaphysis and humeral shaft.
Several biomechanical studies have evaluated the strength of parallel and orthogonal
fixation constructs. Parallel plating of intra-articular distal humerus fractures in patients

with a metaphyseal defect is associated with superior biomechanical properties
compared with orthogonal plating.20, 21, 22, 23
Although biomechanical studies have demonstrated that parallel plating is stronger than
orthogonal plating, clinical studies have found no difference between the two plating
constructs.24,25
In patients with severe comminution of the metaphysis or substantial bone loss, acute
shortening at the fracture site with maintenance of appropriate alignment of the
articular surface should be considered. This may result in enhanced stability of the
fracture, particularly in patients with osteoporotic bone.18 Re-creation of the olecranon
fossa and/or resection of part of the olecranon tip must be performed carefully to allow
for full extension during shortening.
Achieving stable fixation in elderly patients is associated with several challenges because
of osteopenia and poor bone quality. ORIF may be best suited for the management of
fractures with minimal articular comminution in patients with good bone stock.
Treatment of patients with an acute distal humerus fracture via TEA has become
acceptable and preferred, especially in elderly patients (Video 8) .
Type I capitellar fractures usually require ORIF. Mini-fragment, cannulated, or headless
screw fixation from posterior to anterior or countersunk mini-fragment screws from
anterior to posterior can be used. In patients with posterior comminution, supplemental
fixation with a plate and the use of bone graft may be required.5 Type II fractures consist
of articular cartilage with thin subchondral bone, making fixation via lag techniques a
challenge. These usually are managed via anterior-to-posterior screws, bioabsorable
screws, or fragment excision. Aspects of type III fractures that cannot be reconstructed
are excised. Concomitant injuries to the lateral collateral ligament or the radial head may
be present in as many as 57% of patients with a capitellar fracture; therefore, surgeons
should be prepared to manage these injuries at the time of surgery.

Postoperative Management/Rehabilitation
The elbow should be immobilized in a well-padded splint for no more than 7 to 10 days
postoperatively. Extended immobilization is associated with elbow stiffness and should be
avoided unless soft-tissue concerns exist.
If concerns exist with regard to the soft-tissue envelope, then splint immobilization in
extension may help relieve tension on the posterior incision.
Active and passive ROM of the shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand should be initiated
immediately after splint removal. If the soft tissues are tenuous, then elbow motion may be
deferred until adequate healing has occurred.
Patients with an extra-articular fracture should remain non–weight bearing for 6 weeks
postoperatively, and patients with an intra-articular fracture should remain non–weight
bearing for 12 weeks postoperatively.
Resisted extension exercises are avoided until fracture union.

Complications
Elbow stiffness and heterotopic ossification are the most common complications after the
surgical fixation of distal humerus fractures, occurring at a rate of 3% to 42%.
The incidence of postoperative ulnar neuropathy ranges from 10% to 38%; however,
intraoperative management of the ulnar nerve (in situ decompression versus anterior
transposition) remains controversial.
Distal humerus nonunions are more common in patients with an open fracture, an injury with
substantial comminution, or a low transcondylar or intercondylar fracture.
Major wound complications may occur in as many as 16% of patients because of the thin soft-
tissue envelope over the posterior elbow and postoperative swelling.

Complications
Postoperative elbow stiffness and heterotopic ossification are the most common
complications after the surgical treatment of patients with a distal humerus fracture. The
mean postoperative arc of motion ranges from 90° to 106°, and some patients may
experience residual loss of elbow flexion strength of 25%.26, 27 The incidence of
heterotopic ossification ranges from 3% to 42%, and risk factors associated with
heterotopic ossification include head injury, delayed internal fixation, double-plate
fixation, and the use of bone graft or bone substitute.28, 29
Ulnar neuropathy also may occur postoperatively, with the incidence ranges from zero
to 38%.8, 9, 30-32 Symptoms may be transient and are observed postoperatively in
patients with or without nerve transposition. Postoperative ulnar neuropathy may be
related to devascularization after dissection of the nerve; 9, 30 however, many studies
have found no difference between in situ decompression and transposition.8, 31, 33
Nonunion at the distal humerus fracture site occurs in zero to 11% of patients, and risk
factors include fracture comminution, bone loss, unstable fixation, open fracture, and
high-energy injury.2, 3 Patients with a low transcondylar or intercondylar fracture also
have an increased risk for nonunion because maintenance of stable fixation in an area
with limited distal bone stock often is difficult.2

Infection rates range from zero to 14%, and infection is more commonly observed in

soft-tissue envelope and the tension of the wound from postoperative swelling and
elbow flexion.35
Outcomes
In patients with a closed injury managed via ORIF, an arc of motion of approximately 90° to
106° and the return of approximately 75% of flexion and extension strength can be expected.
Loss of elbow extension typically is greater than loss of elbow flexion. Return of functional
elbow ROM (30° to 130°) is the minimum postoperative goal.
Patients with an open distal humerus injury have poorer functional and ROM scores than
patients with a closed fracture.
TEA for the management of acute distal humerus fracture not amenable to stable fixation in
older patients with low functional demands, poor bone stock, or preexisting arthritis may
result in good outcomes and may reduce the rate of revision surgery compared with ORIF.

Outcomes
Union rates after appropriate fixation of distal humerus fractures are excellent (>90%). 2,
36-38 Good to excellent outcomes patient-reported outcomes after the management of
complex distal humerus fractures occur in 82% to 100% of patients based on Mayo
Elbow Performance Index scores.36, 37, 39 Mean elbow extension-flexion arcs after
fixation range from 90° to 106°, and mean pronation-supination arcs range from 150° to
165°.36, 39, 40 Regaining terminal extension is difficult, with a mean extension deficit as
great as 25° reported postoperatively. Residual muscle weakness is common
postoperatively, with strength measurement at 75% compared with the contralateral
healthy side.27 Patients with an open distal humerus fracture have poorer outcomes and
less motion compared with patients with a closed distal humerus fracture.41 Open
fractures also are associated with higher rates of complications, longer time to union,
and higher rates of persistent nerve deficits, requiring additional surgical management.

Long-term outcomes are maintained over time;40 however, radiographic evidence of
posttraumatic arthritis is noted in 80% of patients despite optimal surgical treatment.
TEA should be considered for comminuted intra-articular distal humerus fractures in
women older than 65 years, particularly those with associated comorbidities, such as
systemic steroid use, osteoporosis, or rheumatoid arthritis. Several studies reported
satisfactory outcomes after TEA if stable fixation is not feasible in distal humerus
fractures, particularly in physiologically older patients who have low functional
demands.42-45 McKee et al46 performed a prospective, randomized, controlled trial to
compare the outcomes, complications, and revision surgery rates of 40 patients older
than 65 years with an intra-articular distal humerus fracture managed via ORIF or TEA.
Based on their findings, the authors recommend TEA as a preferred treatment option for
patients with a fracture not amenable to stable fixation. A meta-analysis of 27 studies
comparing TEA and ORIF for the management of distal humerus fractures in patients
older than 60 years reported no difference in elbow motion or functional outcome
scores.47 Major complications and revision surgery were more common after ORIF.
Despite its potential advantages, TEA is associated with disadvantages, including lifetime
weight-bearing restriction and a unique set of complications, such as implant loosening,
instability, periprosthetic infection, periprosthetic fracture, and loss of bone stock, which
make revision surgery extremely challenging and complex. Long-term studies of distal
humerus fractures managed via TEA have reported a revision-free survival rate of 76% to
92% at a follow-up of 10 years; however, at least one-half of the patients in each study
died before final follow-up.48-50
TEA also is a good option for the management of distal humerus nonunions or as a
salvage procedure for failed ORIF.51,52 In a recent retrospective study of patients who
underwent TEA for the management of a distal humerus fracture, no difference in
clinical outcomes, elbow motion, or revision surgery rates were reported between those
who underwent TEA as a primary procedure and those who underwent TEA as a salvage
procedure after failed ORIF. The most common reasons for conversion from ORIF to TEA
were nonunion (36%) and posttraumatic osteoarthritis (32%).

Preoperative CT scans with three-dimensional reconstruction or traction radiographs of distal
humerus fracture may aid in preoperative planning.
Nondisplaced distal humerus fractures or fractures in medically frail, low-demand patients
may be managed nonsurgically; however, close monitoring via serial radiographs is
recommended to assess for interval fracture displacement.
The goals of surgical fixation are anatomic articular reduction, stable internal fixation, and
early range of elbow motion.
Intercondylar distal humerus fractures require plate fixation along the medial and lateral
columns.
Although parallel plating is biomechanically superior compared with 90-90 plating, both
options provide adequate fixation stability, with no differences in clinical outcomes.
TEA should be considered in low-demand elderly patients who sustain a complex distal
humerus fracture that is not amenable to reduction and stable fixation.
Routinely performing ulnar transposition offers no clear clinical benefit but should considered
if the position of the hardware may result in nerve irritation. Care should be taken to avoid
devascularization of the nerve during release.
Stiffness is the most common complication after surgical fixation of distal humerus fractures.
